Now that we have this Zulip I'd like to start a discussion regarding any topics that ought to be discussed in the "About" page but are currently missing. Two that came up in previous discussion:

  • How does Palomar interact with other Mathlib initiative projects like Tau Ceti and Formal Frontiers?

  • What happens to a Palomar registry entry when Mathlib or Lean is updated?

For the second question, my understanding is that each registry entry points to a single version of Lean (and Mathlib), and is not updated with any new version of Lean. Any such revision would require a completely fresh registry entry (or should we allow for the ability to replace previous entries with revised versions?)

Another question to add:

  • My formalization requires axioms beyond the standard set. Can it still be registered?

(I guess the answer is technically "no", but one can rewrite the main statement to explicitly use the form of the axiom as a hypothesis.)

I think an addition to "Why do we need this today?" is something about how it lets people know that a proposed formalisation actually compiles without having to run it themselves.

(This is something important that I think is often overlooked by the more technically savvy parts of the community, who see no obstacle in just running Lean code as they need - for many in the community even navigating Github can be intimidating, let alone learning how to install and run Lean code - but these mathematicians still want to know if they should believe a given formalisation claim or not!)

Another question to perhaps add:

  • I disagree with the AI's assessment of my result as not interesting/noteworthy - what can I do?
    (I expect the answer is 'tough, we trust the AI enough to make good decisions, so if the AI says your result is not interesting it's probably not'. But it would be good to address this up front.)

Terence Tao said:

Any such revision would require a completely fresh registry entry (or should we allow for the ability to replace previous entries with revised versions?)

This hasn't been exercised at all, but in theory when you make a second submission from the same repository/comparator config, this generates a new version with the same Palomar identifier. Palomar doesn't do anything about updating submissions to new Lean or Mathlib versions, but if the original author does, they can resubmit at Palomar and get a new version number.

(Could I ask that someone else takes ownership of turning discussion in this thread into PRs? Such PRs need to edit https://github.com/PalomarRegistry/PalomarWeb/blob/main/about.html. If you ping me I will review/merge such PRs.)

OK, I will draft some PRs for these questions, though for the question "How does Palomar interact with other Mathlib initiative projects like Tau Ceti and Formal Frontiers?" you may be best placed to handle that one.

Submitting various PRs to address the above questions, and also to make a small bugfix that my agent noticed in the process of factchecking the answers.

What happens to an entry when Lean or Mathlib is updated?

Nothing. Each entry verifies one immutable snapshot of a repository against the exact Lean toolchain and the exact dependency revisions that snapshot pinned, and the entry records all of them. Palomar never re-runs a verified entry against a later Lean or Mathlib, so an entry neither improves nor decays as those projects move.

To record a result against newer versions, submit the updated commit and give the existing Palomar ID on the submission form. The new submission is verified and reviewed from scratch, and if it is accepted and you choose to register it, it becomes the next version of that same identifier. The repository, project directory, and Comparator configuration must match the existing entry.

Leave the field blank and the submission becomes a separate entry with its own identifier instead; nothing is inferred from a repository matching an earlier one. Every version stays permanently resolvable at its explicit version URL, while an identifier on its own resolves to the newest active version.

My formalization needs axioms beyond the standard set. Can it still be registered?

Not as axioms. A proved Solution declaration may depend only on the axioms Palomar's current [Comparator configuration policy] permits: in particular sorryAx and Lean.ofReduceBool, which sorry and native_decide introduce, are not among them, and adding them to your own Comparator configuration does not change that. Ordinary decide is fine. The Challenge module, by contrast, is expected to contain sorry.

If a result really is conditional, state the condition instead of assuming it, for instance writing theorem euler_product (h : RiemannHypothesis) : … instead of axiom RiemannHypothesis : ….

I disagree with the review's judgment that my result is not interesting enough. What can I do?

There is no appeal for an individual result: reopening a few decisions for whoever writes in would make the outcome depend on who complained. A rejected submission leaves no public record, and it can be revised and resubmitted after a waiting period. Repeated submissions lengthen that wait steeply, but carry no other penalty.

If you think the [editorial floor] itself is wrong, or you have run into anything else that looks like a defect in Palomar rather than a disagreement about one result, please raise it in the Palomar channel on the Lean Zulip.

Is there a way to leave comments on a registry entry?

Not on Palomar, which does not have the resources to moderate discussion.

The repository an entry points at is the natural home for technical discussion, and most accept issues and pull requests. Beyond that, the registry metadata is dedicated to the public domain under CC0 and published with feeds, so anyone can build a commentary layer over Palomar. However, Palomar does not run or endorse any such site.

Terence Tao said:

OK, I will draft some PRs for these questions, though for the question "How does Palomar interact with other Mathlib initiative projects like Tau Ceti and Formal Frontiers?" you may be best placed to handle that one.

First, let's work out what the question should say, because the current phasing perhaps implies that Palomar is a Mathlib Initiative project (it's not; it's incubated by the Lean FRO and ICARM) and that Tau Ceti is solely a Mathlib Initiative project (it is also incubated by the Lean FRO).

Then some background; I'm not sure whether it is worth saying all this on the About page yet:

There are three types of Lean formalization projects we're seeing at present: libraries (such as Mathlib, CSLib, and Tau Ceti), formalizations of articles or textbooks (as Formal Frontier is working on), and formalizations of individual theorems (whether previously proved in the informal literature, or new).

We intend that Palomar should provide indexing for individual theorems. Established libraries have their own documentation and discovery mechanisms, and don't need separate indexing by Palomar. Further, these libraries are treated as the trusted base providing the definitions needed for easily auditable theorem statements as registered in Palomar. It's okay if people want to make "wrapper" repositories for libraries or book formalizations, with comparator configurations for particularly important theorems, but we don't think its essential that Palomar tries to index everything of this form.

I've merged:

  • Is there a way to leave comments on a registry entry? PalomarWeb#95
  • I disagree with the review's judgment that my result is not interesting enough. What can I do? PalomarWeb#94
  • What happens to an entry when Lean or Mathlib is updated? PalomarWeb#90 (with some minor changes)

I've pushed an edit to

  • About: can a formalization needing extra axioms be registered? PalomarWeb#92.

@Terence Tao, if you're happy with that, I'll merge that too.

So, maybe a question along the lines of "What types of results are suitable for registering with Palomar?", and the answer should be "Individual theorems (which can either be novel, or already proven in the informal literature)", with a suggestion that formalizations of articles or textbooks can go into Formal Frontier, and formalization of libraries could go into Tau Ceti. One could also mention here that Tau Ceti imports are permitted in Palomar (I think - I haven't fact checked this).

The changes look good. A typo:

The repository an entry points at is the natural home for technical discussion

I am not sure what is intended.

Jeremy Avigad said:

The changes look good. A typo:

The repository an entry points at is the natural home for technical discussion

I am not sure what is intended.

Would this version be clearer?

The natural home for technical discussion for a registry entry is the repository the entry points at

(i.e., apply symm :grinning_face_with_smiling_eyes:)

Palomar is not a repository. The mathematics stays in a GitHub repository that is not Palomar’s and remains under its owner’s control; an entry records a claim about one commit of it rather than hosting the development. Palomar does keep a public preservation fork of every registered source, so that an entry does not rot if the original repository disappears.

What external library imports are accepted?

The statement — conventionally Challenge.lean — may import Lean core, Mathlib, and Tau Ceti. Importing Tau Ceti is accepted and marks the entry as having qualified statement dependencies. A project Palomar has already registered is not importable on that basis.

The proof is not restricted this way: dependencies used only by the Solution may be arbitrary pinned Git repositories. The full rules are under [what Comparator requires].

Terence Tao said:

Palomar is not a repository. The mathematics stays in a GitHub repository that is not Palomar’s and remains under its owner’s control; an entry records a claim about one commit of it rather than hosting the development. Palomar does keep a public preservation fork of every registered source, so that an entry does not rot if the original repository disappears.

Dumb question: doesn't that mean that in effect Palomar is a repository?

Ravi Vakil said:

Dumb question: doesn't that mean that in effect Palomar is a repository?

I agree that it sounds a bit like that. How about:
Palomar is a registry, not a repository. The mathematics stays in the original GitHub repository that remains under its owner’s control; an entry records a claim about one commit of it. Palomar keeps a public preservation fork of every registered source, solely as a backup for the registry in the event that the original repository disappears.
It feels a bit wordy, but I can't think of anything better. (It is very tricky, being briefy and pithy, yet complete and responding to all reasonable concerns!)
Yes, it is! I edited it to be a bit less wordy while still (hopefully) getting the point across.
Fair enough, I've updated the relevant PR for this. PalomarWeb#96

hi everyone! sorry I have been AWOL, but the last two days of this congress have been the most intense ones so far, today should be more relaxed and I am starting to catch up and will get to work on whatever I can help with!

(Re: the "keeps a public preservation fork": in practice this is just a pointer in a github database. It has the effect that taking a repository private, or rewriting its history, can not affect our fork. But still in some sense we're not actually "keeping a copy", that's still just Github.)

This is perhaps self-evident, but I propose adding the following additional entry to the About page:

Are AI-generated submissions allowed? Yes. A formalization may be written by a person, produced by AI, or any mixture of the two. The formalization.yaml file must record the automation methods used, including models, framework, and tooling, or manual for formalizations not using any automation.

Additionally, submitters must either be a responsible author or maintainer of the substantive formalization, or have approval from one — see [how to submit].

Hi all. I am a bit surprised that Palomar makes no mention of LeanPool. As described in #Project announcements > Lean Pool -- arXiv-like Lean library @ 💬 , LeanPool is an arXiv-like Lean library. It remains the largest curated formalizations in Lean, containing 148 projects.
LeanPool has the same features as Palomar and more: automated review, project cards as rich as formalization.yaml, profiling, a unified view of all projects. The biggest value-add is maintenance: LeanPool is bumped in lock-step with mathlib.

It seems that at the very least it should be mentioned.

Note that this may be a bug or feature depending on your perspective:

The biggest value-add is maintenance: LeanPool is bumped in lock-step with mathlib.

As I understand it, the bumping is doing by AI, hence without domain expertise. If e.g. Carleson were vendored into Lean Pool, it's not clear to me what would happen if Lean Pool bumps it in some way, but then Carleson itselfs bumps another way. Are you checking for this? (If not, that seems problematic to me.)

if Lean Pool bumps it in some way, but then Carleson itselfs bumps another way. Are you checking for this?

I don't want to highjack this thread and turn it into a discussion about LeanPool. We can discuss further in #general > Discussion for Lean Pool . To answer your question, I am not checking for this. I just checked: out of the 148 projects, 19 have received bumps upstream, so I should be using them. It would be easy to check and use the upstream's version. This is a good idea, I have put it as a TODO item.
